blocks.text: 1. Graph RAG
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447720672-624751657.png

Fusion RAG closed by weighing when its multiplied retrieval cost is worth it. Graph RAG, which retrieves by traversing relationships between entities, introduces a fundamentally different retrieval structure covered as its own dedicated module later in this course.
It walks a knowledge graph of connected entities rather than only ranking isolated chunks, a structural shift explored in full throughout this topic.
2. Chunks Versus Connected Entities
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447720673-762786208.png
Vector retrieval, as covered in Naive RAG's four stage pipeline, treats each chunk as an isolated, independently ranked unit.
Graph RAG instead represents entities and their relationships as a connected structure.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Retrieval structure","How information is represented"],"rows":[["Vector retrieval","Isolated, independently ranked chunks"],["Graph RAG","Connected entities linked by relationships"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Entities And Relationships As The Graph

blocks.alt: Entities And Relationships As The Graph
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447720673-267884862.png
A graph node represents an entity such as a person, product, or company.
A graph edge represents the specific relationship connecting two such entities.
4. Answering Questions Vector Search Cannot Reach

blocks.alt: Answering Questions Vector Search Cannot Reach
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447720673-536765225.png
Much like the multi-hop questions covered in Chain Of Thought, a question needing several connected relationships must be traversed step by step.
A single vector similarity search cannot follow that relationship chain.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A question like which suppliers does the company that acquired our vendor also work with requires following a chain of relationships that a single similarity search over isolated chunks cannot represent.

blocks.text: 5. Building The Graph From Documents
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447720673-816356315.png
Similar to the metadata extraction covered in Document Ingestion, entities and relationships must first be extracted from the raw source documents.
This happens before the graph structure can be queried at all.
6. Traversal Replaces Similarity Search
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447721030-332838899.png
Once the graph exists, retrieval walks outward from a starting entity along its relationships.
This replaces ranking chunks by embedding similarity.

blocks.text: 7. Combining Graph And Vector Retrieval
As covered generally with hybrid search in Retrieval, many real systems combine graph traversal with vector similarity search rather than choosing only one.
Each method covers the gaps the other one leaves open.
8. Graph Construction Is Real Engineering Work
As Advanced RAG covers, each added step costs latency, and extracting reliable entities and relationships from unstructured text takes real upfront effort.
This is a meaningfully larger investment than building a simple vector index.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Reliably extracting entities and relationships from messy source text is a larger upfront engineering investment than embedding chunks into a vector index, a cost worth weighing before committing to graph RAG.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Graph RAG Earns Its Graph Construction Effort

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Graph RAG Earns Its Graph Construction Effort
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447721031-281936741.png
Data with rich, explicit relationships between entities suits graph RAG well.
Loosely related, standalone documents, by contrast, rarely justify building a graph at all.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Building a graph for data that has few meaningful relationships between entities.
Underestimating the engineering effort required to reliably extract entities and relationships.
Choosing graph traversal alone instead of combining it with vector search where useful.
Skipping the entity and relationship extraction step and expecting the graph to build itself.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Graph RAG retrieves by traversing relationships between entities, not just ranking chunks.
Vector retrieval treats chunks as isolated units; graph RAG connects entities and relationships.
Graph nodes represent entities; graph edges represent the relationships between them.
Questions needing several chained relationships are reachable by traversal, not similarity search alone.
Entities and relationships must be extracted from source documents before the graph can be queried.
Traversal walks outward from a starting entity along relationships instead of ranking by similarity.
Many real systems combine graph traversal with vector search to cover each other's gaps.
Reliable graph construction takes meaningfully more upfront engineering than a simple vector index.
